title: Data Collection Facts Label
text:
Data Source Facts Label














Source Identity






Source name


2020 Residential Energy Consumption Survey (RECS) Public Use Microdata File, version 7 (Jan 2024), U.S. Energy Information Administration. https://www.eia.gov/consumption/residential/data/2020/index.php?view=microdata




Domain/topic


Energy (residential energy consumption and housing)




Source type


Government dataset (federal statistical survey, public-use microdata)











Collection Context






Collector/producer


U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA), the statistical and analytical agency within the U.S. Department of Energy (public, federal). The Household Survey was conducted with private contractors IMG-Crown and RTI International; the Energy Supplier Survey with private contractors Leidos and Westat.




Original purpose


Periodic national survey to provide detailed information about energy usage in U.S. homes: a reference-year snapshot of energy characteristics, usage patterns, and household demographics. Used for public reporting (data tables, reports) and as input to EIA’s sector-level projections such as the Annual Energy Outlook.




Collection method


Combination of methods: (1) voluntary, self-administered Household Survey (form EIA-457A) by web or paper, in English or Spanish, mailed to an address-based sample; (2) mandatory Energy Supplier Survey (EIA-457D-G) where utilities and fuel suppliers submitted billing/delivery records via a web form or Excel file; (3) engineering-based end-use models calibrated to billing totals; (4) weather data from NOAA Climate Data Online linked to each home. Missing survey answers filled by hot-deck imputation.




Record-creation event


A sampled household completes the Household Survey (at least 7 of 10 key questions answered). The record is then linked to that household’s supplier billing data, modeled end-use estimates, and weather data.











Observation and Scope






Unit of observation


One occupied housing unit used as a primary residence (one responding household), identified by DOEID.




Population or objects represented


All occupied housing units used as primary residences in the 50 states and DC (about 123.5 million). Excludes vacant homes, seasonal/second homes, and group quarters (dorms, nursing homes, prisons, barracks); housing units on military installations are included. Sample: 18,496 responding households.




Time period covered


Consumption and expenditures cover calendar year 2020 (Jan 1 - Dec 31, 2020). Household Survey fielded Sept-Nov 2020 and Jan-Apr 2021. Supplier data collected July 2021 - March 2022, covering bills from March 2019 - Feb 2021. Final file released January 2024.




Geographic area coverage


United States: all 50 states and the District of Columbia. Public file includes census region, census division, state, climate region/zone, and urban/rural type; addresses and localized geography are removed.











Variables and Data Structure






Main variables/fields


Housing characteristics (housing type, year built, square footage); appliances and electronics; space heating, air conditioning, and water heating equipment and fuels; thermostat settings; lighting; household characteristics (number of members, income, own/rent); energy assistance; electric vehicles and solar; telework/online school (COVID); heating and cooling degree days; annual consumption and cost by fuel (electricity, natural gas, propane, fuel oil); end-use consumption estimates (e.g., space heating, cooling); sampling weight NWEIGHT and 60 replicate weights.




Data types included


Numerical (consumption, cost, square footage, degree days, weights, counts); categorical (coded survey responses, income ranges, fuel and equipment types); IDs (DOEID); geographic categories (state, region, climate zone); imputation flag variables. No GPS, image, or audio data.




Direct measurements


Respondent-reported answers (e.g., number of household members, housing type, thermostat setpoints, laundry loads per week); supplier-reported billed energy consumption and dollars spent (for households with billing data); weather-station temperatures used to compute degree days.




Possible proxy variables


Modeled end-use consumption estimates; heating and cooling degree days; climate region/zone; year-built range; household income category; urban/rural type; energy insecurity / energy assistance questions.











Documentation






Documentation found


Variable and response codebook (XLSX); ‘Using the microdata file to compute estimates and standard errors’ guide; Household Characteristics Technical Documentation Summary; Consumption and Expenditures Technical Documentation Summary; Square Footage Methodology; ‘Comparing the 2020 RECS with previous RECS’ report; survey forms EIA-457 A-G; RECS FAQs and terminology pages.




Stated collection details


Address-based sample from the USPS delivery file, stratified by state (about 99.6% expected frame coverage). Up to six mailings over about six weeks; $10 incentive for web response. 18,496 completes: 72.8% web, 27.2% paper; median web completion time 32 minutes. Response rate 38.6% unweighted / 37.9% weighted (state range 30.4% NY to 50.7% WI). About 240 public-file variables had imputed values (median imputation rate 2.7%, range 0-22.1%). Supplier survey: 94% of suppliers responded; 84% overall household account coverage (about 50% for propane and fuel oil). For electricity, 83% of households had complete billing data and 14% had none; households with no billing data had consumption imputed from models. Survey answers were edited to reconcile with billing data (e.g., main heating fuel). Weights adjusted for eligibility, nonresponse, and poststratification to 2020 Census and 2019 ACS totals; 60 jackknife replicate weights. Wood use is self-reported only and not included in totals. Confidentiality protected under CIPSEA; addresses removed and some variables top-coded.

Data Source Facts Label














Source Identity






Source name


Building Energy Benchmarking




Domain/topic


Energy and Water Consumption




Source type


Government Dataset











Collection Context






Collector/producer


District of Columbia Department of Enerfy and Environment (DOEE)




Original purpose


To track and public dissclose energy and water performance of buildings under Washington DC’s Benchmarking law




Collection method


Enerygy Star, Adminstrative benchmarking progarm




Record-creation event


Required Annual Submition of energy and water consumption











Observation and Scope






Unit of observation


Individual building/properties reporting a record annually




Population or objects represented


Public and Private Buildings in Washington DC




Time period covered


2012-2025




Geographic area coverage


Washington, District of Columbia via city/state/Zip code











Variables and Data Structure






Main variables/fields


Property ID and name, reporting year, report status, address, owner, ward, year built, property type, floor area, ENERGY STAR score, energy-use intensity, greenhouse gas emissions, water use, natural gas use, electricity use, latitude/longitude, verification information, and enforcement action




Data types included


Numerical, categorical/text, dates/timestamps, geographic coordinates, and identifiers




Direct measurements


Electricity use, natural gas use, water use, building floor area, geographic location, year built, and monthly electricity/natural-gas consumption




Possible proxy variables


Energy Star score, site EUI, property type, building size,greenhouse-gas emissions











Documentation






Documentation found


Data.gov




Stated collection details


Annual Benchmarking record, records marked as “In Compliance”, “Data Under Review by DOEE”, “Exempt from this year’s disclosure”, “No Report Received”, or “Incomplete Report”

title: Data Collection Facts Label
text:
Data Source Facts Label














Source Identity






Source name


EIA Monthly Electric Power Industry Report (2010-current)




Domain/topic


Energy Use




Source type


Public government dataset











Collection Context






Collector/producer


U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA)




Original purpose


Monitor electricity industry conditions and trends.




Collection method


Monthly surveys of retail sales of electric utilities and electricity service providers.




Record-creation event


Monthly reporting cycle with provider reports that EIA processes and combines into a record for each state and month.











Observation and Scope






Unit of observation


One state during one month, with separate numbers for each electricity customer sector.




Population or objects represented


Retail electricity sales in the residential, commercial, industrial, and transportation sectors.




Time period covered


January 2010–July 2026




Geographic area coverage


All 50 U.S. states and the District of Columbia











Variables and Data Structure






Main variables/fields


Electricity sales, Year, month, State, Data status, Electricity revenue per sector, Customer count, Average price




Data types included


Numerical; categorical, dates




Direct measurements


Providers report electricity sales, revenue, and customer counts




Possible proxy variables


Electricity sales may map to electricity usage per state











Documentation






Documentation found


EIA’s dataset description, EIA-861M survey form and instructions




Stated collection details


Collection occurs monthly, and reporting is mandatory for respondents

title: Investigating a Dataset’s Ingredients
text:
Our team chose energy usage, with a focus on how the rapid buildout of AI data centers is affecting the power grid around it.
Data centers have always used a lot of electricity, but the push to train and run AI models has sped up construction dramatically over the past few years. A single large facility can draw as much power as a small city, and utilities in some regions have started planning new generation and transmission just to keep up. At the same time, there’s been growing public concern that everyday customers could end up covering part of that cost through higher electricity bills.
We picked this topic because it sits right where technology and everyday life meet. As computer science students, we spend a lot of time thinking about what AI can do, and much less time thinking about what it takes to physically power it. The topic also has clear stakeholders across government (the U.S. Energy Information Administration, state utility commissions), research and academia, and nonprofits focused on energy affordability, which made it a good fit for finding well-documented public data.

title: Investigating a Dataset’s Ingredients
text:
Research Question

Has energy usage or pricing significantly increased in places where data center buildout for AI is prevalent?

title: Investigating a Dataset’s Ingredients
text:
Our Approach
Each team member independently found a different public dataset related to this question and documented how it was collected using a Data Collection Facts Label, similar to a Nutrition Facts Label but for data. The labels cover who produced each dataset, why and how it was collected, what one record represents, and what time period and geography it covers.
You can view each label here:

Joseph Callaway
Pano Klironomos
Logan Roche

We then compared the three sources side by side to decide which one fits our research question best, looking at trustworthiness, relevance, ethical concerns, and scope. That discussion is on the Comparative Analysis page.
